name: Campaign Creation
content:
STEP 1: WORLDBUILDING

Before you begin, have a quick discussion about campaign tone, themes, and omissions so everyone starts with shared expectations. Start your campaign notes with these expectations.

1) START WITH A MAP

Whether you're building your world entirely from scratch or working from an existing concept, pick a MAP that represents the scope of the campaign, whether it's a whole world, a region, or a city. Choose a map that the group finds compelling and evocative—something you can return to again and again as an anchor for the story you're telling.

2) DEFINE "THE RECENT UPHEAVAL"

Looking at your map, decide what RECENT UPHEAVAL broke the long isolation of the Ancestries of this world. Did a natural phenomenon remove a physical barrier? Did some hardship cause populations to relocate? Did some new threat push refugees out of their homeland? Did the discovery of some new resource draw out the adventurous?

The Recent Upheaval can be absolutely anything you want it to be—good, bad, somewhere in-between, whatever you choose. All that matters is that there is a reason why peoples long separated are now mixed together. The scale of that mixing is up to your group. It might be worldwide, focused within one region, or even concentrated in a single city.

Consider these questions: How long ago did it happen? Did it happen all at once or gradually over time? What discoveries and conflicts arose as it happened? To what extent is it still happening?

Describe all this in your campaign notes.

3) PLACE CULTURES

While Ancestries in the world of Renaissance have been spread around and mixed together by The Recent Upheaval, CULTURES are tied to a physical location. Choose which Cultures you'll be including in your campaign, and place each of them on the map.

Most Cultures lend themselves to being presented as discrete places, but their proximity to—or even overlap with—each other is up to you. As you place them on the map, ask questions: Why does this Culture exist here and not elsewhere? What is its relationship with its neighbors, near and far? How has its physical location influenced it?

In a campaign with a narrower scope (small region, city), it may be more appropriate to establish each Culture's relation to the immediate setting rather than placing discrete Cultural focal points on the map: When did people originally from each Culture migrate into this area? Are they spread around or have they formed an enclave? To what degree does Culture of origin matter in this area?

As you add Cultures to the map, don't just place them—discuss and tinker. Add routes between important locations, add small places by the wayside, name natural landmarks and points of interest. If something sparks the group's interest, give it a name and put it on the map. If something is better represented in your campaign notes than on the map, be sure to record it there.

A map is "ready" when the whole group is excited about and interested in the world, but there are still plenty of gaps to be filled and mysteries to be investigated. Don't be afraid to leave space; a full map is overcooked.

OPTIONAL WORLDBUILDING METHODS:

The above steps are just a broad scaffolding for worldbuilding, and while this may be enough for some groups to work with, other approaches are absolutely welcome. The game mechanics of Renaissance do not require that you follow any particular worldbuilding method. Many great minds have produced excellent worldbuilding tools and games. Any process that produces a vibrant world that's ready to explore is valid, and will serve the purposes of this game.

In addition to the many wonderful resources available, Renaissance offers two further options:

1) For a lengthy, in-depth exercise that will produce a rich world history, try Whole Cloth.

2) For a simple conversational approach, try this Statement, Question, Answer format:

  • As above, start with a map and choose the Cultures for your campaign.

  • Establish a turn order by rolling dice or by any other method you choose.

  • Player 1 starts by making a STATEMENT about the world. This statement could place a Culture or place name on the map, describe an aspect of an existing feature, describe an event (past or present), or something else. The player has full sovereignty in this moment and gets to shape the world. Once they have made their statement, they should pause to allow other players to ask clarifying questions, which are very much encouraged.

  • Player 1 then asks a QUESTION about the world. This can be related to the statement they just made or an unrelated topic. The question is directed at Player 2.

  • Player 2 ANSWERS the question. Again, they have full sovereignty in this moment to shape the world. After answering, they should pause to allow clarifying questions, which again are very much encouraged.

  • Player 2 then makes a statement, beginning the cycle anew. They follow it with a question for Player 3, who answers, then makes a statement, then poses a question for Player 4, etc.

  • At the end of each round, the group should consider whether the world is ready for a campaign.

STEP 2: SET THE STAGE FOR ADVENTURE

MAKE A LIST OF CAMPAIGN QUESTIONS

Now that you’ve built your world, it’s time to decide what stories you want to tell in it. What parts of the world spark the most interest in your group? What are you curious about? What mysteries do you want to investigate?

As a group, make a LIST OF QUESTIONS you have about the campaign world. Keep the list concise. One or two questions per person is great. More than two questions per person is probably too much. You’ll be adding questions to this list as you play, so it’s good to leave room for new ones later on.

Record your list in your campaign notes or on your map.

QUESTIONS BECOME QUESTS

Each question on your list will serve as a potential jumping-off point for a QUEST in the campaign.

A Quest is a chapter within the campaign that seeks to answer one (or sometimes more than one) of the group’s questions about the campaign world.

To pick your first Quest, discuss as a group. Which question is most exciting or seems like a good starting point? Who feels inspired to act as Game Maestro (GM) for that Quest? Pick a question and pick a GM.

You can choose to pick more than one question for a given Quest if the questions are intertwined in some way, but beware of making the scope of the Quest too broad. Having a clear goal for each Quest is key. If a question is too broad or vague to provide a clear objective for a Quest, work together to narrow it down.

ROTATING GM ROLE

The GM role may rotate with each Quest. How often the role shifts is up to your group. Nobody has to be GM if they don't want to, but each member of the group is encouraged to consider running a Quest at some point in the campaign. The world gets more interesting when more of us get a chance to shape it.

While the GM for each Quest will necessarily develop and hold secret information about the campaign world as part of running the Quest, any such secrets that do not come to light in the course of the Quest do not persist into subsequent Quests, and subsequent GMs have full latitude to make their own decisions about the campaign world - including things previous GMs may have decided but never revealed to the group.

While maintaining public, group-authored campaign notes is highly encouraged, developing a hidden-lore "campaign bible" that gets passed from GM to GM is discouraged. If a GM wants to shape the world, they need to do it within scope of the Quest they're running by revealing that information to the players. As the campaign evolves, everyone at the table builds shared understanding of the world together.

To put it plainly:

  • Deciding something about the campaign world while GM and bringing it into the game makes it true.

  • Deciding something about the campaign world while GM and keeping it secret does not mean that it's true.

ROTATING CHARACTERS

The world of Renaissance is about the collision and mixing of peoples and ideas. Just as each Quest helps us answer a question about the campaign world, each character offers a different lens through which to view that answer. Additionally, in a practical sense, a rotating GM role necessitates at least a partially shifting cast of characters for each Quest.

As such, while a player can only bring one character at a time to a Quest, each player is allotted a stable of up to three player characters. The player has full sovereignty over these characters' decisions, feelings, and actions, and they may only be included in a Quest if the player chooses.

At the outset of a campaign, each player should only create one character. Subsequent characters should be created and introduced with care and purpose. Avoid introducing more than one or two new characters per Quest unless circumstances require more.

If a player already has three characters in their stable, they must retire one before creating a new character. Players may choose to retire a character under their care at any time. The player can choose one of two paths for the character:

  • The character is written out of the story entirely. The character can never again be brought back into the story, though their impact on the world will persist.

  • The player forfeits their sovereignty over the character and allows them to become a part of the broader campaign world. This means that the character can never again be a player character. However, the character may still be involved in the story in some way, whether on the fringes or directly involved in the action as an NPC piloted by the GM.

It’s worth noting that creating more than one character is entirely optional; a player may choose to stick with one character for the duration of the campaign, and that's totally fine.

In all this, work together to find the right balance for your group. Character creation is fun. Introducing a new character into a campaign can inject life into gameplay. But doing so too often can over-widen the focus of the campaign or make existing characters seem less significant. On the other hand, all good stories have endings, and being able to end one character’s story while allowing others’ to continue is a powerful tool. As the campaign progresses, keep talking about what’s working for your group and what’s not.
